Law School Admission Council 662 Penn Street, Newtown PA 18940-0040 LSAC P: 215.504.1466 Email: registrar@lsac.org Dear Colleague: This Law School Report includes a transcript of the candidate's enrollment during Spring 2020 and/or subsequent semesters during which the COVID-19 pandemic affected students' education. The COVID-19 pandemic emerged in early 2020, and the response of many higher education institutions was to convert mid- semester to online education and to announce changes in their traditional grading systems. During Spring 2020, Fall 2020 and subsequent semesters, many students were faced with unanticipated changes in the circumstances of their enrollment. During Spring 2020, students on residential campuses were in many cases required to leave campus with little advance notice; students on spring break were instructed not to return to campus. Many international students either could not leave campus or could not return to their home countries. As the Fall 2020 semester began, schools that may have planned for in-person classes were forced to pivot to online or hybrid classes with very little notice to students. The disruption to students' lives from the rapid change in their physical and learning environments may have included effects on physical or mental health, financial security, and access to academic resources and support services. Notably, many colleges and universities changed their grading systems. Some converted to a mandatory Pass/Fail (or similar) system, others permitted students to choose whether to receive traditional or Pass/Fail grades, still others retained their traditional grading systems. This letter is included in the Law School report as a reminder of the unusual and difficult circumstances surrounding enrollment during the period of time when the COVID-19 pandemic presented a barrier to traditional learning. Law school admission staff may wish to take these circumstances into account. Sincerely, LSAC Credential Processing LSAC.org

LSAC X Candidate Name: Alex Kennington Candidate ID: 44173071 Date: 2024-11-17 Prompt ID: WPBA027-01 Writing Prompt Privatizing Scientific Research Democratic governments typically fund and oversee a large portion of scientific research in the defense, health, space, and energy industries. Privatization involves transferring the management of a service or activity from the government to organizations in the private sector, as we've seen happen with the growth of charter schools and for-profit prisons. In evaluating whether to privatize a government program, consideration must be given to the most efficient use of resources and the proper scope of government, of course-but the market incentives of the private sector should also be weighed against the government's mandate to ensure the public good. These complicated aspects of privatization raise interesting questions regarding the funding, management, and control of scientific research. KEY QUESTION: To what extent, if any, should the management and funding of scientific research be privatized? Read and carefully consider the arguments presented in the following perspectives. Each suggests a particular way of thinking about the issue captured in the Key Question. Perspective 1 - an excerpt from a speech by a philanthropist It's a modern idea to think that science should be funded and managed by the government. Historically, science was supported by wealthy patrons; thus, we owe some of our greatest discoveries and breakthroughs to privately funded research. Not that we should fully revert to the private-patron model, but people tend to be unduly skeptical of private incentives. Sure, most private corporations are primarily concerned with profits, but some do fund basic research for its own sake. Moreover, there are also many privately funded nongovernmental organizations driven by more altruistic motivations, including foundations that seek cures for understudied diseases. Many private-sector individuals fund science simply because they want to advance human knowledge and promote scientific discoveries. It's time to return to a model where the bulk of scientific research funding comes from altruistic patrons, thereby freeing up taxpayer resources. Perspective 2 - an excerpt from a report by a consumer advocate We all know the adage "Never trust a salesperson." The truth behind it is why we should severely limit, or even disallow, corporate-funded and -managed scientific research. When large sums of money are at stake, the reality is that companies just cannot be trusted to either (1) pursue socially beneficial innovations or (2) consistently communicate the truth to the public. In the first case, consider the potential business impact of innovations that disrupt industries. For example, the plastic bag industry, estimated to generate over $10 billion annually in the United States alone, has no incentive to disrupt their own business by developing an environmentally sound alternative to plastic. In the second case, private-sector incentives sometimes work against truthfulness. For example, if the corn farming industry wants to sell more corn, it can fund a "scientific" study that, regardless of its findings, is presented in a way that skews results in favor of the benefits and value of corn in all its varied applications. Corporations regularly leverage

misinformation and scientific-sounding propaganda to increase their bottom line. Most individual consumers do not have the kind of training, time, or skill it takes to identify which studies lean on poorly designed experiments and misleading statistics. A government that allows the private sector to continue to pay for and manage scientific research is nearly as bad as a government that allows fraud and deception. Perspective 3 - an excerpt from a government research report There's nothing wrong, in principle, with allowing both private and public funding and management of scientific research, provided that we properly regulate private-sector research. Private-sector research often fails to include peer review, in which other qualified researchers in the field evaluate a study's research methods and results to ensure they are credible and valid. Private-sector research, then, is often simply subpar. By contrast, government grants and funding for science often come with requirements to produce carefully peer-reviewed research. Moreover, research funded by the government seldom comes with an agenda influenced by profits. Instead, the goal is research that will further advance human knowledge and benefit society. The funding goes where the representatives of the people tell it to go, whether it be researching clean energy or cures for diseases, or solving various public health problems. Even defense- and military-related research is geared toward a just end: the safety of the people. Given the obvious conflict of interest between maintaining peace and profiting from military conflict, we should not exclusively trust the private sector with defense. Better regulation of private-sector research could not only help advance science but also help keep private interests out of key government functions. Perspective 4 - an excerpt from an interview with a pharmaceutical entrepreneur I have no problem with public money going to private researchers, but I'm strongly opposed to government-managed scientific research because it is incredibly difficult to make sure its funding is being used efficiently. Government oversight requires paying people to perform such oversight. Therefore, funding designated primarily for scientific research must also pay for all sorts of managerial work, such as processing paperwork, awarding funds, and ensuring compliance with government standards. None of that oversight is itself the science that is allegedly being funded. Just give the money directly to private research outfits that have the infrastructure already in place to use the funding most efficiently! Prewriting Analysis: Generating Ideas for Your Argumentative Essay Spend the remainder of your prewriting time working through the prewriting questions presented below. These questions are intended to help you think critically about the issue and generate productive ideas for your essay. Record your thoughts in your digital scratch paper by making notes or lists, or by writing short answers to the questions. Your notes in response to the prewriting questions will still be available to you while you write your essay, but they will not be evaluated or included as part of your essay. These questions are strictly provided to help guide your analysis of the perspectives and to help you develop your own argument in response to the Key Question. Prewriting Questions Which perspective(s) do you find most compelling? What relevant insights do you see in the perspective(s)? What principles or values do you see at work in the perspective(s)? What strengths and weaknesses can you find in the perspective(s)? Your argument should incorporate or address ideas from at least one of the perspectives provided. In addition, your own knowledge, experiences, and personal values can be valid sources of evidence, and you can include these in your essay: What knowledge do you already have about this issue? Consider information you have read or heard, including things you've learned at home or school, etc. What values influence your position on this issue? Consider your worldview or belief system, as well as any guiding principles or convictions you hold. What experiences do you have that might be relevant to this issue? Consider any personal experience you might have with this or similar issues, or other relevant lessons learned from your own life. Response:

Scientific research should be privatized as much as possible as long as the government oversees that this research is peer-reviewed and accurate. The biggest ethical issue with privatization when it comes to funding research and science is that companies are driven by profit which can be contradictory to truthfulness, accuracy, and altruism. However, the unethical outcomes that can occur from private research are not much different from the ones that can occur from government research. It may seem like governments are held to higher standards, but this is often untrue. Private companies have to follow local, state, and federal laws and are often held to high ethical standards due to the stock market and consumer's expectations. Although, a private company could spread misinformation or skew data to push out an agenda that would sell its products better, this happens often in politics. "Never trust a politician" is an adage as old as "never trust a salesperson", and in America political speech is the least regulated speech. Politicians can also be influenced by interest groups or by constituents to skew research as well. As long as private-sector research is peer-reviewed, it would be just as trustworthy as public-sector research. It would relieve taxpayers, increase efficiency, and allow individuals who are passionate about solving certain issues to flourish and better society. Although companies have to make money to exist, the majority have bigger ambitions than that. Companies have mission statements and value sets. Sam Walton created Walmart with the mission statement, "Save Money, Live Better", and he truly wanted to bring the items that people needed to their town at a fair price. Mark Cuban wanted Americans to be able to buy medication at an affordable, so he created an online pharmacy to give consumers transparency on fair prices. Elon Musk created a way that rockets could go to space without being destroyed, unlike NASA, which helps scientists and engineers save money and be more efficient. In many cases, individuals who are passionate about solving issues have altruistic intentions and flourish in the private sector where they can pursue their own ideas, create their own companies, and reap the profits from their hard work. Governments rely on individuals that might not have this passion and might only want to solve certain issues because they have to for the sake of the public. The private sphere is not only just as trustworthy, it is often more efficient and better equipped to handle scientific research - and it should.

William Fulbright College of Arts & Sciences Department of English Letter of Recommendation for Alex Kennington It is my great pleasure to write this letter of recommendation for Alex Kennington, who was a fantastic student in an undergraduate English course that I taught at the University of Arkansas. Alex performed at the highest level in that class, and it was truly an honor to get to work with her. In the fall of 2024, I got to know Alex while she was enrolled in my course "Communicating Effectively on the Needs of Women Who Are Leaving Prison and Reentering Society." Alex was extremely reliable, almost never missing a class meeting and always being prepared to discuss course material or to collaborate with others on group work assignments. Also impressive was the quality of work that Alex submitted for the course, starting with the short paper/presentation assignment she completed, focusing on an article I had assigned to her, "The Period Project: The Fight for Menstrual Equity in Prisons," written by staff members at the California Women's Law Center and published in Ms. Magazine. Alex skillfully analyzed the authors' rhetorical strategies to support her evaluation of the text's overall strengths. She identified the multiple target audiences of the piece, its main purpose, and the specific ways in which it appealed to pathos, ethos, and logos-for example, she noted the quality and quantity of outside sources referenced to bolster the text's credibility, the "appeals to the reader's empathy by emphasizing how harsh and humiliating the conditions are for incarcerated women during their menstrual cycles," and the use of statistical research to "support the claim that nonprofits would not be able to mitigate the situation [since] it is a legislative issue." As a result, Alex's final assessment of the article as "powerful," as well as "useful" to members of our class who might want to return to it later in the semester when working on other course assignments, was very persuasive. The main paper that Alex wrote for the course was likewise researched thoroughly and developed very effectively, boldly focusing on a topic that was important but also one that we had not had the time to discuss in depth as a class: the needs of LGBTQ+ individuals, specifically queer women, who are returning to society from prison. In my feedback to Alex, I wrote that she did "an excellent job finding and referencing a range of authoritative sources as well as proposing a detailed and feasible strategy for supporting these women" living in the Northwest Arkansas area. Truly, Alex's suggested solution-a three-pronged approach that would entail college students' serving as mentors, networkers, and sensitivity trainers-was exceptional. The final major assignment for the course was a slide presentation, and Alex once again submitted superb work. Building upon the idea she researched for her major paper assignment, Alex designed content for her presentation slides that was professional, relevant, authoritative, creative, and feasible. She used her project to pitch an original program she called Arkansas Legal Allies. She explained how ALA would "combat the lack of in-house legal services" at an existing reentry support program for LGBTQIA2S+ individuals, Beyond These Walls (BTW), located in the Pacific Northwest. Alex explained how ALA could arrange for pre-law undergraduate students at the University of Arkansas to help BTW by virtually "conducting research, summarizing reports, drafting documents, and proof-reading," work that would eventually be passed along to and used by full-time legal professionals hired by the organization. Alex deftly located and referenced this program to help her audience envision how her own proposal could be equally effective at helping returning individuals navigate society while providing undergraduate students at the U of A a unique chance to prepare for a law career-I'm still amazed by how she went above and beyond with her completion of the final assignment for the course. I am familiar with the strength of Alex's qualifications for law school through the work she did in my course, but I'll quickly mention that I'm also aware that Alex's reputation as being highly talented and accomplished extends well beyond the boundaries of my own classroom. As you will undoubtedly see in Alex's other application materials, she maintained an extremely high GPA as an undergraduate and not only majored in Political Science but also minored in Rhetoric, Legal Studies, and Business Management. She also worked with both the Office of Career Connections and the Office for Sustainability on our campus, held multiple leadership positions, and volunteered with the EMPOWER Program. All this to say: Alex is not only an extremely smart, capable, and well- rounded person; she is also, without question, a caring individual. For all of these reasons, and the ones I mention above, I recommend Alex without reservation for any law program to which she applies: she will do a beautiful job in that graduate program, just as she has done in her undergraduate program. Thank you for considering Alex's application to your school. If I can be of further assistance, please feel free to contact me at 479-856-8899. Alex carries herself with a quiet reserve, but beneath that calm demeanor is sharp intellect and steady confidence. She is meticulous in her work, pays close attention to detail, and consistently delivers high-quality products. Her consistency and thoughtful approach will serve her exceptionally well in law. Her commitment to advocacy is evident by her push for sustainability and public education around environmental responsibility on campus. Through her work in the Office for Sustainability, she managed outreach efforts, created educational graphics, wrote blog posts, coordinated data collection, and even led the campus Sustainability Coalition. I regularly saw her tabling, educating students, and breaking down complex topics into approachable language which will translate directly to legal communication. In the Career Influencer program, she contributed in a major way by producing campus-wide media, interviewing employers, and educating students about career resources. She was reliable, punctual, and thoughtful in her approach. What stands out most is her ability to remain personable and grounded while doing high-level work. Alex educates compassionately, advocates with service in mind, and leads with steadiness. Alex embodies qualities that define excellent future attorneys: she is analytical, community- oriented, articulate, and deeply motivated by purpose. She will be a thoughtful student, a strong contributor to any academic community, and a lawyer who uses her voice to uplift others. I give her my full and confident recommendation. LSAT Score Information All LSAT tests are valid and reliable predictors of law school success because they are all composed of questions from the same banks, and all questions are continuously reviewed by experts to ensure quality, reliability, and validity. All test sections include approximately the same number of questions and cover the same content areas of analytical reasoning, logical reasoning, and reading comprehension. The score scale is 120-180 for all tests. The LSAT (including the LSAT-Flex) is the only test specifically designed to predict first-year performance in law school. The LSAT is supported by decades of empirical evidence verifying its efficacy in predicting first-year law school performance by testing skills rated by law professors as most important to classroom success. Percentiles provided with all scores are based on the previous three-year period. LSAT (5 sections), June 1991 to May 2020 The LSAT using the current 120-180 scale was administered from June 1991 through April 2020, and it consisted of four scored sections and one unscored section. Tests were administered in person at test centers. All scores earned during this period will be averaged together. (Earlier versions of the LSAT, using a different score scale, were offered between 1948 and 1991.) LSAT-Flex, May 2020 through July 2021 The LSAT-Flex was administered from May 2020 through July 2021, and it consisted of three scored sections and no unscored section. The LSAT-Flex was designed in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. Tests were administered online with live remote proctoring. Scores on the LSAT-Flex will be averaged with other LSAT-Flex scores and with the four-section LSAT described below beginning in August 2021. LSAT (4 sections), From August 2021 The LSAT, beginning in August of 2021, consists of three scored sections and one unscored section, administered online with live remote proctoring. Scores earned on this LSAT and on the LSAT-Flex will be averaged together.
